# The life of a vehicle {#sec-lifecycle}

```{r}
source("R/book.R")
ps <- read_pipeline("outputs", "quality", "pca_status_by_year.csv")
```

The CARS data follows each vehicle through its life, year by year. To read it
correctly you need to know the stages a vehicle passes through, which ones
leave a trace in the data, and how the data describes the years in which a
vehicle is not seen.

## Stages of a vehicle's life

### A new vehicle

A new vehicle is registered with the DVLA when it is first sold, or sometimes
earlier by a dealer (*pre-registration*), and receives its registration
number. Its **date of first registration** is recorded by the DVLA and its
**first-use date** by DVSA; the two are usually the same. The **manufacture
date** can be months earlier for a vehicle that sat in stock.

For its first three years (four in Northern Ireland) a new vehicle needs no
MOT. Until its first test, the MOT data knows it exists but not where it is or
how far it has been driven. Once it has been tested, the annualisation fills
in its early years from that first test (see below).

### An imported vehicle

A used vehicle imported into the UK is registered when it arrives. It is given
a plate for its age, where its age can be shown, or a Q plate where it cannot
(@sec-number-plates). Its UK registration date can therefore be many years
after it was built, which affects anything inferred from dates, such as its
Euro standard (@sec-fuels-emissions).

### The first MOT

At three years old the vehicle has its first MOT (@sec-mot-test), and from
then on it is observed at least once a year: its location (the postcode area
of the test station) and its odometer reading. The first test also gives the
first measurement of how far it has been driven: the whole distance since new.

::: {.callout-note .todo title="To be written"}
Whether the data can identify vehicles tested before their third birthday
(taxis, private hire vehicles and others), and how they appear in the
mileage figures.
:::

### Off the road: SORN

A keeper who takes a vehicle off the road, and stops taxing and insuring it,
must make a **Statutory Off Road Notification** (SORN). A SORN vehicle may not
be driven or parked on a public road, and needs no MOT. A SORN lasts until the
vehicle is taxed again, sold or scrapped.

A SORN vehicle therefore drops out of the MOT data, and reappears if it returns
to the road. Many old vehicles stay on SORN for years, which is why DfT's
counts, which include SORN vehicles, hold more old vehicles than the MOT data
(@sec-data-quality).

::: {.callout-note .todo title="To be written"}

had to be renewed every twelve months rather than lasting indefinitely

[Impact assessment 2013/188](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukia/2013/188/pdfs/ukia_20130188_en.pdf)).
:::

### Export

A vehicle sold abroad is *marked for export* and leaves the UK register. The
DVLA records the marker (`markedForExport_DVLA`, `ever_export_marked`).

### End of life

A vehicle at the end of its life is taken to an **authorised treatment
facility**, which issues a *certificate of destruction* and tells the DVLA. A
vehicle that is badly damaged may be written off by its insurer, and either
scrapped or repaired and returned to the road. Some vehicles are stolen and
never recovered.

## How the data describes a vehicle's life

For every year from 2005 to 2025 the vehicle table has a column `pca_YYYY`.
Where the annualisation could place the vehicle, it holds a postcode area.
Otherwise it holds one of three statuses:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| a postcode area (e.g. `LS`) | **Observed**: the vehicle is placed in this area that year |
| `unborn` | The vehicle had not yet been first registered (its birth year is this year or later) |
| `unknown` | The vehicle existed, but was not placed: for example a new vehicle that has not yet had its first MOT, or a long gap between tests |
| `dead` | The year is after the vehicle's last MOT and beyond the years its postcode area is carried forward |

::: {.callout-important title="Pitfall: observed does not mean tested that year"}
The annualisation gives a vehicle a postcode area in years when it was not
tested:

- **before its first MOT**, the postcode area of the first test is copied back
  to the years since its first registration;
- **after its last MOT**, the postcode area is carried forward for about two
  years.

So a vehicle is *observed* from its first registration, once it has been
tested, until about two years after its last test. A vehicle scrapped soon
after its last MOT therefore stays *observed* for about two more years. The
pipeline's `quality/pca_observation_by_year.csv` counts, for each year, the
observed vehicles that were past their last MOT or under three.
:::

::: {.callout-note .todo title="To be confirmed"}
The exact rules for copying the postcode area back from the first test and
forward from the last, from the Bristol team.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-pca-status
#| fig-cap: "Vehicles in the CARS vehicle table by their status in each year."
long <- rbind(
  data.frame(year = ps$year, status = "Observed", n = ps$pca),
  data.frame(year = ps$year, status = "Unknown", n = ps$unknown),
  data.frame(year = ps$year, status = "Dead", n = ps$dead),
  data.frame(year = ps$year, status = "Unborn", n = ps$unborn)
)
long$status <- factor(long$status,
                      levels = c("Observed", "Unknown", "Dead", "Unborn"))
ggplot(long, aes(year, n, colour = status)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cars_cols) +
  scale_y_count() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Vehicles") +
  theme_cars()
```

Every vehicle is in exactly one status each year, so the four lines in
@fig-pca-status always add up to the same total: every vehicle in the table.
The *observed* line peaks before the end of the series and then falls. That
fall is not a shrinking fleet. Vehicles first registered in the last three
years mostly have not had a first MOT yet, so they are `unknown`, and the last
year, 2025, is incomplete.

::: {.callout-important title="Pitfall: dead means no longer tested, not scrapped"}
A vehicle is `dead` in every year after its last MOT, whatever the reason:
scrapped, exported, declared SORN, exempt as a historic vehicle, or simply
driven illegally without a test. The data cannot tell these apart. A vehicle
that comes back from SORN after a gap is `unknown` in the gap, not `dead`,
because the status is set from the date of its last test.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Pitfall: the recent years look like vehicles are vanishing"}
A vehicle tested for the last time in 2023 might be dead, or might simply be
late for its test. Near the end of the series the data cannot yet tell, so a
vehicle last seen in either of the final two years is usually left `unknown`
rather than `dead`. Treat counts of vehicles leaving the fleet in the last two or
three years with care.
:::

## Within-year flags from the annualisation

The Bristol team's annualisation (@sec-sources-linkage) also sets, for each
year, flags describing where the vehicle was in its life on 1 July, the
*straddle date* used to assign each year:

- `is_new_vehicle`: in its first-use period, before its first MOT;
- `is_intertest`: between two MOT tests, with a test either side of 1 July
  that are no more than two years apart;
- `is_end_use`: in its last period, after its final MOT.

The flags are blank before the vehicle is born, more than a year after its
last test, and when the tests either side of 1 July are more than two years
apart. Take a vehicle first used in September 2007 whose first test on record
is in 2013, with later tests in 2014, 2016, 2018 and every year from 2020. It
went six years without a test, and there are gaps of 26 months (2016 to 2018:
too long, so `is_intertest` is blank) and 23 months (2018 to 2020: under two
years, so `is_intertest` is TRUE).

Mileage is still shared out across every year between two tests, however long
the gap. The flags describe the evidence, not whether a mileage exists.

The CARS pipeline uses these flags to find each vehicle's last MOT year (and
so when it becomes `dead`), and then drops them from the published vehicle
table.
